sendha namak.explanation: Rock salt, used during Hindu fasting (regular table salt is avoided).
sendha namak.whereToFind: Any Indian grocery store, or Amazon

kala namak.explanation: Black salt — sulphurous, tangy, used in chaat and raita.
substitutes: sea salt plus a pinch of amchur

kasuri methi.explanation: Dried fenugreek leaves. Adds a distinctive earthy aroma to North Indian curries.

hing.explanation: Asafoetida — a pungent resin that replicates the flavour of onion and garlic. Essential for Jain cooking.
substitutes: garlic powder plus onion powder (if not Jain)

ghee.explanation: Clarified butter with the milk solids browned off — nuttier than butter and stable at high heat.
substitutes: coconut oil for a vegan version
ghee.whereToFind: Most supermarkets, any Indian grocery store

jeera.explanation: Cumin seeds. Usually bloomed in hot fat at the start of a dish.

haldi.explanation: Ground turmeric — earthy, faintly bitter, and the source of the yellow colour.
substitutes: a pinch of saffron for colour only

dhaniya.explanation: Coriander — seeds or ground. Mild, citrusy, and the bulk of most masala blends.
substitutes: ground cumin plus a little lemon zest

garam masala.explanation: A warming blend of cinnamon, clove, cardamom and pepper, added near the end of cooking.
substitutes: allspice plus a pinch of cinnamon
pumpkin pie spice at a pinch
garam masala.whereToFind: Most supermarkets, any Indian grocery store

methi dana.explanation: Fenugreek seeds — bitter and maple-scented; a few go a long way.

ajwain.explanation: Carom seeds — thyme-like and sharp, often added to breads and fried snacks to aid digestion.

chaat masala.explanation: A tangy finishing blend with black salt, amchur and cumin. Sprinkled on, never cooked.
substitutes: lemon juice plus a pinch of salt and cumin

amchur.explanation: Dried green mango powder, used to add sourness without adding liquid.

sabudana.explanation: Tapioca pearls. A fasting staple because it is not a grain.
substitutes: small tapioca pearls from an East Asian grocer
sabudana.whereToFind: Any Indian grocery store, or an Asian supermarket

poha.explanation: Flattened rice flakes that soften in moments — the base of a common breakfast.
substitutes: rice flakes from an Asian grocer
quick-cook rolled oats as a loose stand-in

moong dal.explanation: Split mung beans — the lightest and quickest-cooking dal, easy to digest.

toor dal.explanation: Split pigeon peas — the everyday dal across most of India.

urad dal.explanation: Split black gram. Gives idli and dosa batter its lift, and dal makhani its body.

chana dal.explanation: Split brown chickpeas — nutty, holds its shape, needs longer cooking.

masoor dal.explanation: Red lentils. Cooks down to a soft purée in fifteen minutes.

besan.explanation: Chickpea flour. Used for batters, and as a thickener in kadhi.
besan.whereToFind: Most supermarkets, any Indian grocery store

atta.explanation: Finely milled whole wheat flour for rotis — softer than Western wholemeal.
substitutes: wholemeal flour sifted with a little plain flour

maida.explanation: Refined white flour, used in naan, samosa pastry and bakery items.

suji.explanation: Semolina — coarse wheat, the base of upma and sooji halwa.

paneer.explanation: Fresh unaged cheese that holds its shape when cooked and never melts.
substitutes: firm tofu for a vegan version
paneer.whereToFind: Most supermarkets, any Indian grocery store

curd.explanation: Plain unsweetened yoghurt, thinner and tangier than Greek style.
substitutes: plain yoghurt thinned with a little water
coconut yoghurt for a vegan version

coconut milk.explanation: Pressed coconut cream and water — the base of most coastal and Kerala curries.

tamarind.explanation: Sour fruit pulp that gives sambar and rasam their backbone.
substitutes: lime juice with a little brown sugar
tamarind.whereToFind: Any Indian grocery store, most supermarkets

jaggery.explanation: Unrefined cane sugar with a mineral, molasses-like depth.

kokum.explanation: A dark, sour dried fruit rind used in Konkani and Gujarati cooking instead of tamarind.

kadhi patta.explanation: Fresh curry leaves — nothing like curry powder; citrusy, added to hot oil.
substitutes: a strip of lime zest as a distant stand-in
kadhi patta.whereToFind: Indian grocery stores (buy fresh and freeze)

tejpatta.explanation: Indian bay leaf — cassia-scented, closer to cinnamon bark than a Mediterranean bay leaf.
substitutes: a small piece of cinnamon bark

saunf.explanation: Fennel seeds — sweet and aniseed-like; also chewed after meals.

elaichi.explanation: Green cardamom pods — floral and warm, used in both sweet and savoury dishes.
substitutes: a mix of cinnamon and clove

laung.explanation: Whole cloves — intensely aromatic; two or three flavour a whole pot.

dalchini.explanation: Cinnamon or cassia bark, usually added whole to hot fat.

kesar.explanation: Saffron threads, steeped in warm milk before use.
substitutes: a pinch of turmeric for colour (not for flavour)

khoya.explanation: Milk reduced until it is solid — the base of many Indian sweets.
substitutes: full-fat milk powder mixed with a little cream
khoya.whereToFind: Indian grocery stores and sweet shops

boondi.explanation: Tiny fried chickpea-flour pearls, soaked into raita or soaked in syrup for laddoo.
substitutes: omit, or use crushed plain crackers in raita

sev.explanation: Crisp chickpea-flour noodles scattered over chaat as a topping.

papad.explanation: A thin lentil wafer, roasted or fried, served alongside a meal.

raw banana.explanation: Unripe banana — the standard Jain replacement for potato, since it grows above ground.
substitutes: potato (only if root vegetables are allowed)

suran.explanation: Elephant foot yam. Accepted by many Jain families even though it grows underground — check with the cook.

tendli.explanation: Ivy gourd — a small crisp gourd, common in Gujarati and Jain kitchens.

dudhi.explanation: Bottle gourd — mild and watery, used in everyday sabzis and in kofta.

arbi.explanation: Taro root — starchy and slightly slippery; a common fasting vegetable.
substitutes: baby potatoes (if root vegetables are allowed)

kuttu.explanation: Buckwheat flour. Not a grain, so it is allowed during Hindu fasts. Gluten free.
substitutes: buckwheat flour from a health-food shop

singhara.explanation: Water chestnut flour — another fasting flour, mild and pale.

rajgira.explanation: Amaranth — a fasting pseudo-cereal, sold as flour or puffed seed.

sama ke chawal.explanation: Barnyard millet. Looks like rice but is not a grain, so it is fasting safe.

makhana.explanation: Puffed lotus seeds — light and crunchy when roasted, common during fasts.
